[package]
name = "yetlet"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
repository.workspace = true
description = "HTML-first Rust framework with explicit optional native capabilities"
readme = "README.md"
include = ["src/**", "guides/**", "tests/**", "examples/**", "README.md", "LICENSE-*", "Cargo.toml", "Cargo.lock"]

[features]
default = ["html"]
html = []
actions = ["dep:serde"]
reactive = []
server-axum = ["html", "dep:axum", "dep:serde", "dep:tower"]
request-id = ["server-axum"]
session = ["server-axum", "dep:cookie", "dep:getrandom", "dep:subtle"]
auth = ["dep:axum"]
auth-session = ["auth", "session"]
session-redis = ["server-axum", "dep:tokio", "dep:redis", "dep:serde", "dep:serde_json", "dep:getrandom", "dep:sha2", "dep:subtle"]

config = ["dep:serde", "dep:toml", "dep:dotenvy", "dep:libc"]
secrets = ["dep:secrecy"]
secret-provider = ["config", "secrets"]
signing = ["dep:openssl", "dep:openssl-sys", "dep:foreign-types", "dep:serde"]
rate-limit = ["dep:axum", "dep:tower", "dep:governor"]

[dependencies]

# yetlet::actions

**Experimental `0.9.0-alpha.5`, unpublished.** Requires Rust 1.99 or newer. This is one of Yetlet's sixteen library candidates; use the local checkout rather than assuming a registry release. APIs are pre-public, and bounded prototype verification is not production qualification.

`yetlet::actions` defines typed semantic commands and explicitly selected executors. It does not forward DOM events or create a persistent remote event circuit. The portable contracts select serde. Browser HTTP execution is separately selected by `yetlet-browser` feature `actions`; import `yetlet_browser::actions::HttpExecutor`.

## Choose an executor

Implement `Command` with an associated `Response`, then select an `ActionExecutor<C>`. `LocalExecutor::new(handler)` accepts a synchronous `Fn(C) -> Result<C::Response, ActionError>` and exposes it through async `execute`. Local commands and results need no serialization; the caller owns the handler's captured state. Futures intentionally have no `Send` requirement.

`HttpExecutor::new(path)` validates an explicit same-origin absolute path. Construction and `endpoint()` are available natively, but HTTP execution is implemented only on WASM. That implementation requires serde input and a deserializable response, sends a JSON POST, and decodes the result. The [shared Todo commands](../../../examples/todo-ui/src/lib.rs) and [browser dispatch caller](../../../examples/todo-browser/src/lib.rs) demonstrate both paths. Follow [Todo setup](../../../examples/todo-server/README.md), or run from the repository root with its browser prerequisites:

```bash
cargo xtask build browser
cargo run --locked -p yetlet-todo-server
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000/app`; local toggle and remote Create have separate owners and execution boundaries.

## Errors and application responsibilities

Invalid endpoints fail with `ActionError::InvalidEndpoint`. Query/fragment syntax, protocol-relative URLs, backslashes and ASCII controls are rejected. Fetch/decoding failures report `Network` or `InvalidResponse`; non-2xx results report `Remote { status, code }`, with the typed error envelope used when decodable. Local/domain errors retain their explicit variants.

No automatic retry, application timeout, cancellation protocol, authentication or CSRF token attachment is provided. The server must validate inputs, authentication, authorization and CSRF policy; serialization alone provides none of those guarantees. A retired UI lifetime must suppress late results explicitly, as the Todo caller does.

[Custom transport research](../../../docs/YT-024-CUSTOM-TRANSPORT-RESEARCH.md) proves one app-owned typed TCP adapter over this existing trait. It does not select a supported transport/plugin framework or change the default browser HTTP path.

## License and compatibility

Dual-licensed under [MIT](../../../LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](../../../LICENSE-APACHE). The privately prepared `0.1.x` policy preserves documented behavior and Rust 1.99 in patches; public activation remains blocked. See [compatibility](../../../docs/COMPATIBILITY.md), [API classifications](../../../docs/API-CONTRACTS.md) and [developer guides](../../../docs/README.md). Links to companion packages and records assume this checkout; they do not imply public hosting or distribution.

# yetlet::auth

Install native identity resolution only on selected routes. Authentication
establishes a verified identity; business authorization remains application-owned.

**Experimental, unpublished.** Use this source checkout and the documented target scope.


## Prerequisites

Use Rust 1.99+ and this unpublished source checkout. Select `yetlet::auth`
explicitly in a native Axum application. Supply a resolver, its typed state,
an anonymous-response closure and resource authorization. The wiring below
assumes a fallible setup function; it is not a listener or a real login provider.
Enable `auth-session` only for the separately documented Memory bridge.

## Minimal integration

### Native composition

Depend on this crate explicitly, then apply native Axum/Tower middleware only
to selected routes. Required extraction is `Authenticated`; optional extraction
is `Option<Authenticated>`. Both read the layer's private resolved state, without
consuming the body. State injected into the authentication layer is separate
from native handler State; ordinary application structs and Arc handles work.

This compiling wiring example deliberately resolves everyone as anonymous and
has a deny-by-default application policy. Replace the resolver with a maintained
provider's verified result and the policy with authoritative resource checks.
No submitted identity becomes trusted merely by calling the constructor.

```rust
use axum::{
    Router, http::{StatusCode, request::Parts},
    middleware::from_fn_with_state,
    response::{IntoResponse, Redirect}, routing::get,
};
use yetlet::auth::{
    Authenticated, Authentication, Principal, ResolveFuture, authenticate,
};

fn resolve<'a>(_parts: &'a mut Parts, _state: &'a ()) -> ResolveFuture<'a> {
    Box::pin(async { Ok(None) })
}
fn authorize(_principal: &Principal, _resource: &str) -> Result<(), StatusCode> {
    // No explicit application allow means denial.
    Err(StatusCode::FORBIDDEN)
}
async fn private_page(identity: Authenticated) -> Result<&'static str, StatusCode> {
    authorize(identity.principal(), "account")?;
    Ok("Private account")
}
let authentication = Authentication::new("application", (), resolve, || {
    Redirect::to("/login").into_response()
})?;
let app: Router = Router::new()
    .route("/account", get(private_page))
    .route_layer(from_fn_with_state(authentication, authenticate::<()>));
# Ok::<(), yetlet::auth::InvalidAuthenticationInput>(())
```

The same layer works with `App::route_layer`; no dependency on the server adapter
is needed in this crate's normal graph. Register routes before their layer;
sibling groups remain independent. Duplicate resolver layers on one request
produce a generic 500; nested authorization layers reuse the resolved identity.
Native Router 404/405 and middleware ordering rules remain authoritative.

## Expected result

The shown resolver returns `Ok(None)`: a request to the assembled `/account`
scope selects the explicit `/login` redirect, rather than granting access. The
example constructs no `/login` page. A real verified principal still needs the
application authorization check; the policy shown defaults to denial.

## Configuration and errors

### Principal and resolver

`Principal::from_verified(issuer, subject, authentication_name, tenant)` accepts trusted,
already-verified input and checks only shape. Nonempty, non-whitespace-only,
control-free values have these UTF-8 byte limits, without normalization or
truncation: issuer 2048, subject 255, authentication name 64, optional tenant 255.
Invalid inputs return value-free `InvalidAuthenticationInput`; the same error
covers invalid `Authentication::new` registration configuration. Provider-specific
protocol/claim rules are additional obligations. Getters expose only those four
fields; `same_identity` compares exact issuer+subject, independently of
authentication name/tenant.
Debug redacts identity. There is no serde, Default, View or implicit principal
extraction from public extensions, headers or browser state.

`authentication_name()` returns the application-configured authentication
registration/resolver label, with the byte bound `MAX_AUTHENTICATION_NAME_BYTES`.
It is not an HTTP `WWW-Authenticate` protocol scheme, issuer, storage-backend type
or permission. Matching uses the exact configured string, without normalization.
The fixed Display message is `invalid principal or authentication scheme`;
it includes no rejected values. Both constructors return `InvalidAuthenticationInput`.

`Resolver<S>` is a borrowed Parts/state function returning `ResolveFuture`:
`Result<Option<Principal>, Response>`. One boxed future is used per installed
request; configuration/state is shared through Arc. These are selected costs,
not a zero-overhead claim for installed authentication.

| Resolver result / condition | Effect |
|---|---|
| `Ok(Some(principal))` with the selected authentication name | Required/optional extraction succeeds; application authorization is still required |
| `Ok(None)` | Optional extraction returns None; required extraction calls the explicitly supplied anonymous-response closure |
| `Err(response)` | Stops the request; invalid credentials, malformed input and unavailable services must remain errors, even on optional routes |
| No installed layer, duplicate layer, mismatched principal authentication name | Generic 500, never anonymous or a handler call |

The resolver must validate credentials, enforce its validity/freshness bounds,
return redacted responses (normally 400 malformed, 401 invalid credentials,
503 unavailable), and never fall back to a weaker provider. Authentication
errors and application policy errors are native responses; no result hierarchy
or policy engine is added. A raw Principal extension is removed before
resolution. This private-state boundary protects against untrusted request
assertions; it cannot sandbox malicious application/provider middleware.

Failure mapping is explicit. An HTTP 401 needs a nonempty applicable
`WWW-Authenticate` challenge; a missing/empty challenge fails closed to generic
500. The application owns complete challenge syntax and applicability: the
crate does not implement an HTTP authentication scheme. A cookie/form consumer
may explicitly select a local 303 login redirect instead. No Basic/Bearer
challenge, redirect, identity-header parser or permission is installed by default.
Never redirect outages, policy denial or attacker-controlled return URLs.

Every response inside the selected scope, including errors and redirects, is
`Cache-Control: no-store`; existing Set-Cookie, Vary and other headers survive
ordinary processing. Response bodies remain streaming. Explicitly choose
escaped display data for SSR; never render Principal or credentials. The
application/provider owns error/log redaction, authorization and any CSRF,
cookie, revocation or policy service; successful extraction grants no business
access. An uncertain/failed policy lookup must not turn into an allow.

### Boundaries

YT-114 tests a synthetic resolver, not a production login protocol. Distributed Session
bridging, real OIDC, cookie changes, account storage, refresh/revocation services
and provider-specific operational qualification are outside this crate's
current scope. [YT-115](../../../docs/YT-113-123-OPT-IN-CAPABILITIES.md#yt-115--optional-session-and-cookie-authentication-bridge)
was separately selected at the Memory bridge scope. Existing Session APIs and
no-JS form support are preserved; asynchronous Redis bridging remains unselected. The release candidate's original supported package set is unchanged;
this crate remains unpublished with publication-prepared metadata and intentionally refuses wasm32 compilation.
Baseline apps do not depend on it, initialize its state or execute its layer.

### Optional Memory Session bridge

Enable `features = ["auth-session"]` explicitly. Compose existing Session middleware
**outside** `authenticate`: the Session extension must exist before resolution.
The `session::memory` helper reads the server-owned reference synchronously and
calls your identity mapping; no Session ID or Principal is automatically stored
in browser state. Unknown/expired cookies may already have become new anonymous
records according to Memory's existing contract. An in-flight retired record
uses your selected failure response; provider unavailability is always 503 and
a missing Session layer is 500, including on optional routes.

```rust
# #[cfg(feature = "auth-session")]
# fn example() {
use axum::{http::{StatusCode, request::Parts}, response::{IntoResponse, Redirect}};
use yetlet::auth::{Principal, ResolveFuture, session};
#[derive(Clone, Default)]
struct IdentityRef { account: Option<String> }
fn resolve<'a>(parts: &'a mut Parts, enabled: &'a bool) -> ResolveFuture<'a> {
    Box::pin(async move {
        session::memory::<IdentityRef>(parts, |record| {
            let Some(subject) = record.account else { return Ok(None) };
            if !*enabled || subject != "account-one" {
                return Err(StatusCode::FORBIDDEN.into_response());
            }
            // This reference came from protected server-owned Session state.
            // A real app performs current authoritative account mapping here.
            Ok(Some(Principal::from_verified("urn:app:accounts", &subject, "memory", None).unwrap()))
        }, || Redirect::to("/login").into_response())
    })
}
# }
```

Login verification, CSRF before mutations, replace-and-rotate on login and
revocation on logout stay explicit. Authorize resources independently and
recheck current Session/account policy at sensitive business commit boundaries.
The qualified HTTP fixture uses live process-local account policy and serializes
logout/writes; it supplies no cluster-wide revocation or production IdP guarantee.
No async rewrite or Redis dependency is added to the foundation.

## API reference

See [Auth source/rustdoc](../src/auth/mod.rs), the [Memory helper](../src/auth/session.rs) and
the [current API reference](../../../docs/API-REFERENCE.md). Rustdoc setup context
lines beginning with `# ` support example compilation; embed the actual wiring
in your own fallible setup function instead of copying them as Rust statements.

<details>
<summary>Historical delivery context and evidence</summary>

Unpublished, experimental, explicitly selected **native** identity foundation.
It implements the [YT-113 contract](../../../docs/YT-113-AUTHENTICATION-CONTRACT.md)
at the bounded [YT-114 scope](../../../docs/YT-114-IMPLEMENTATION.md). It verifies no
credentials itself and installs no default Session, Cookie, OIDC or Bearer provider.
The separately enabled `auth-session` feature adds a bridge to existing Memory Session;
see [YT-115 evidence](../../../docs/YT-115-SESSION-AUTH.md).

</details>

`yetlet::html` serializes a `yetlet-core::View` into escaped HTML on native Rust. Its only dependency is `yetlet::view`; it installs no HTTP server or browser runtime.

## Render a View

Call `render_to_string(&view)` to receive `Result<String, RenderError>`. Text and attribute values are escaped; `escape_text` is also available for text escaping. Build the View using `Element` and `View` from core. The complete [Hello World handler](../../../examples/hello-world/src/lib.rs) uses this path through the server adapter. From the repository root:

```bash
cargo run --locked -p yetlet-hello-world
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:3003/hello/World`. Use `yetlet-server-axum::Page` when you need a complete HTTP document with strict CSP; this serializer itself returns a fragment and owns neither response headers nor document metadata.

## Policy and errors

[YT-110](../../../docs/YT-110-DOM-CAPABILITIES.md) adds duplicate-name and selected control-child errors to the pre-public `RenderError` contract. Supply each attribute once, do not nest forms inside a View, and use text children for textarea/option. The serializer normalizes textarea CRLF/CR to LF and preserves an initial newline after HTML parsing; callers must remove any former manually prepended newline sentinel. Live values, selectedness and reset are browser/application behavior, not a serializer binding runtime.

`RenderError` distinguishes invalid tag/attribute names, forbidden attributes, unsafe URL schemes and children on void elements. Names follow the lowercase identifier policy; `script`, `style`, `iframe`, `object` and `embed` tags are rejected. Attributes beginning with `on`, plus `style` and `srcdoc`, are forbidden. Selected URL attributes reject script/data schemes conservatively, including whitespace/control obfuscation. There is no raw HTML escape hatch.

The serializer borrows a View for the call and returns an owned String; no mount or disposal lifetime exists. It buffers the complete fragment rather than streaming. Escaping is not a complete URL-policy engine or an accessibility checker: callers still choose semantic markup and application URL policy. The HTML and DOM subsets differ, so successful HTML serialization does not prove browser mount compatibility.

# yetlet::rate_limit

Apply native endpoint/group rate limits using explicit per-process memory
budgets. Configuration reuse and shared accounting are separate choices.

**Experimental, unpublished.** Use this source checkout and the documented target scope.


## Prerequisites

Use Rust 1.99+ and this checkout. Select the limiter in a native Tower/Axum
application; choose a trusted key and intended route scope. The Rust wiring is
a setup fragment inside a fallible function, not a complete server. The existing
`native` example additionally selects the optional Settings loader as an example
dependency; its external settings are documented below.

## Minimal integration

For a complete listener-free configuration check, from the repository root:

```sh
cargo run --locked -p yetlet --features rate-limit,config --example rate-limit-native -- --check
```

The following existing fragment instead installs a limiter directly; compiling
or loading settings does not select that installation automatically.

### Shared budget wiring

```rust
use axum::{Router, http::request::Parts, routing::get};
use std::time::Duration;
use yetlet::rate_limit::{Budget, InvalidRateLimitInput, Key, Policy as RateLimitPolicy, RateLimitLayer};

let refill_interval = Duration::from_secs(2);
let policy = RateLimitPolicy::new(refill_interval, 5, 64)?;
let shared = Budget::new(policy);
let layer = RateLimitLayer::new(shared, |_: &Parts| {
    Ok(Key::new("group-total").expect("bounded constant"))
});
let app: Router = Router::new()
    .route("/first", get(|| async { "first" }).route_layer(layer.clone()))
    .route("/second", get(|| async { "second" }).route_layer(layer));
# Ok::<(), InvalidRateLimitInput>(())
```

## Expected result

The wiring installs one shared Budget/key on `/first` and `/second`: the initial
burst is five and one cell refills every two seconds. Deficits return 429;
capacity/internal failures return 503 as detailed below. Separately, the runnable
native example defaults off. Its `--check` prints `Configuration valid; listener not started.`
and exits without binding; ordinary native mode listens on port 3000.

## Configuration and errors

### Admission, ownership and errors

`Policy` is immutable reusable configuration. Each `Budget::new(policy)` starts
independent accounting. Cloning a Budget, layer or service shares accounting.
The same Budget and same key across routes/methods create a group total; adding
a route/method to the key intentionally partitions it. Attach native
`MethodRouter::route_layer` after registering methods to preserve 404/405;
native GET includes HEAD. Later-added methods are not automatically covered.
Intentional stacked layers each charge once, without cross-layer refunds.

Governor 0.10.4 implements GCRA: the example policy initially admits five
requests, then refills one cell every two seconds. It is not a rolling-window
request count. Keys contain 1–512 bytes; retained key capacity is 1–4096.
Refill interval/burst must be nonzero and their checked product at most one day.
Invalid Policy or Key construction returns the value-free unit error
`InvalidRateLimitInput`. Key Debug output is redacted.

A synchronous extractor reads immutable request Parts and returns a Key or a
native Response. It never receives the request body. Choose an explicit fixed
key, actual transport peer metadata, or a verified typed account extension
installed by earlier authentication. Account encodings must distinguish the
relevant issuer, tenant and account, independently of session rotation. Missing
required metadata must reject. Arbitrary Forwarded/X-Forwarded-For headers are
not trusted or parsed; there is no fallback identity or built-in Auth lookup.
An account limiter after authentication does not protect authentication cost.

A private mutex covers lookup, cleanup, capacity, admission and post-success
clock sampling. Entries are reclaimed only after a full refill duration since
the last successful check's subsequent monotonic timestamp. Rejection never
refreshes retention. Existing keys remain serviceable at capacity; new keys
return 503 when no fully replenished record can be reclaimed. Cleanup is bounded
and opportunistic, with no background task. Dropping all handles releases state.

Validated time snapshots protect Governor's unchecked nanosecond arithmetic.
A Budget fails closed after 100 × 365 days of age, on backward/unavailable clock
samples, or on poisoned state. A post-admission clock failure also fails closed;
it does not refund. The horizon is deliberately far below the dependency's
approximately 584-year representation limit and leaves room for refill debt.

Deficits return generic 429 with `Cache-Control: no-store` and a finite
`Retry-After` rounded up to seconds, at least one. The hint is an opportunity,
not reserved credit. Capacity/internal failures return generic no-store 503
without Retry-After. Extractor rejections retain their status, body and other
headers and receive no-store. Native downstream responses/errors, readiness and
backpressure are preserved. There is no body buffering, waiting for refill or
refund after errors/cancellation. SSE is charged at connection admission.

### Opt-in Settings loader in the native example

The example explicitly selects the existing [yetlet-config loader](../../../docs/CONFIGURATION.md)
as a **development/example dependency**. Configuration is not a Core service or
limiter runtime dependency. The application calls `Loader::load` once at startup,
deserializes its own `Settings` type, and composes the native routes. No framework
provider registry, per-request configuration lookup or ambient library setting
is introduced. The root workspace excludes the nested config/secrets workspaces
so they retain their isolation. In the shared root lockfile, config's existing
exact libc pin resolves libc from 0.2.190 to 0.2.186; it adds no normal Settings
dependency to the limiter or server. See the YT-117 follow-up evidence for the
explicit version delta and focused compile check.

The [application-owned base TOML](../examples/rate_limit/settings/base.toml) declares:

```toml
enabled = false

[policy]
interval_ms = 2000
burst = 5
max_keys = 64
```

The loader reads this explicit manifest-relative settings directory, overlays the
selected finite profile and applies environment overrides. The prefix is
`RATE_LIMIT`; absent `RATE_LIMIT_ENVIRONMENT` selects Production. Development,
Staging and Production all keep rate limiting disabled unless explicitly enabled.
The example names its startup constructor `build_rate_limit_policy()` and aliases
the public `yetlet::rate_limit::Policy` as `RateLimitPolicy` at the application
boundary. This makes construction and capability explicit without renaming the
public crate API or changing the settings schema.

The Rust settings field is `refill_interval_ms`, with
`#[serde(rename = "interval_ms")]` preserving `policy.interval_ms` and
`RATE_LIMIT_POLICY__INTERVAL_MS` as the external names. They specify
the refill interval for **one cell**, not a counting window or the full burst
refill duration. There is no `policy.refill_interval_ms` wire key or environment
alias. Explicit environment snapshots use `Loader::load_with_env`.

The application settings structs reject unknown fields. Missing files, unknown
keys, malformed TOML and invalid scalar types fail startup according to the
existing loader contract, including when rate limiting is disabled.

| TOML field | Environment override | Base default |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED` | `false` |
| `policy.interval_ms` | `RATE_LIMIT_POLICY__INTERVAL_MS` | `2000` |
| `policy.burst` | `RATE_LIMIT_POLICY__BURST` | `5` |
| `policy.max_keys` | `RATE_LIMIT_POLICY__MAX_KEYS` | `64` |

The earlier flat example keys `RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL_MS`, `RATE_LIMIT_BURST` and
`RATE_LIMIT_MAX_KEYS` are replaced by the nested policy keys above. The existing
loader rejects these old, now-unknown prefixed keys rather than silently ignoring
them. Boolean overrides accept exactly `true` or `false`.

Enabled mode validates positive refill interval/burst, retained capacity 1–4096
and checked refill interval × burst at most one day before binding. Disabled mode still
loads and type-checks settings, then returns the original native routes without
constructing Policy/Budget/layer, invoking extraction, accounting or pruning.
Type-valid unused policy values do not activate or construct a limiter.

Run from the repository root:

```sh
cargo run -p yetlet --features rate-limit,config --example rate-limit-native -- --check
RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=true RATE_LIMIT_POLICY__BURST=2 \
  cargo run -p yetlet --features rate-limit,config --example rate-limit-native -- --check
RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=true cargo run -p yetlet --features rate-limit,config --example rate-limit-native
```

`--check` validates startup settings and exits before opening a listener. Without
it, the example listens on `127.0.0.1:3000`; Ctrl-C shuts it down. `/first`
(GET/HEAD/POST) and `/second` (GET/HEAD) share the loaded policy and the same fixed
Budget/key; `/public` is unmetered. A Policy reused with a separately constructed
Budget would instead retain independent accounting.

The limiter library never reads files or environment variables. Changing settings
requires restart. No hot reload, throughput measurement or benchmark is included;
a later benchmark can select `enabled = false` for native unmetered routing.

Budgets are per process and reset on restart or deliberate reconstruction.
There is no shared/Valkey counter, cluster quota, WAF/DDoS guarantee or production
capacity claim. Body, concurrency and connection limits remain separate
application choices. The example quotas are illustrations, not deployment
recommendations.

## API reference

Use [limiter source/rustdoc](../src/rate_limit/mod.rs), the [native example](../examples/rate_limit/native.rs)
and the [current API reference](../../../docs/API-REFERENCE.md). The `# Ok` line is
rustdoc context; place wiring in your own fallible setup function.

<details>
<summary>Historical delivery context and evidence</summary>

An experimental, unpublished, native-only Tower/Axum admission layer for
[YT-117](../../../docs/YT-117-RATE-LIMIT.md). Explicit installation is required;
Core, the server facade, Auth and browser applications do not enable it.

</details>

# yetlet::reactive

**Experimental `0.9.0-alpha.5`, unpublished.** Requires Rust 1.99 or newer. This is one of Yetlet's sixteen library candidates; use the local checkout rather than assuming a registry release. APIs are pre-public, and bounded prototype verification is not production qualification.

`yetlet::reactive` provides an optional synchronous local message/reducer/commit graph. It is renderer-neutral and has no dependencies, I/O or server/browser runtime. Add it only to surfaces that need explicit local update ownership.

## Use the implemented graph

Construct `LocalGraph::new(state, reducer, commit)`, obtain a weak read/dispatch handle with `handle()`, and call `dispatch(message)` or `batch(messages)`. Both `graph.snapshot()` and `handle.snapshot()` return an owned clone of the published state. `subscribe(observer)` returns an owned subscription: retain it while notifications are needed.

Read through the weak handle when a callback needs state without capturing the
strong owner. Before any dispatch, snapshot reads the initial state without
rendering or notifying. Inside a reducer/commit callback it reads the previous
published state; inside an observer it reads the newly published state. A
re-entrant dispatch queues work, so an immediate read does not imply that queued
work has completed. Snapshot does not flush or run callbacks itself.

The internal borrow ends before `State::clone`; arbitrary clone code can
re-enter the graph and controls its own side effects. Clone may share
interior-mutable application data, so this is not a deep-copy or freshness
guarantee after return/await. The handle stays weak; a returned value adds no
graph ownership beyond its own application data. The
[YT-105 snapshot slice](../../../docs/YT-105-GRAPH-SNAPSHOT.md) records the bounded
contract and verification, including Todo/Admin adoption. Todo's local executor
reads the handle after dispatch; Admin reads it before constructing a save.
Their separate committed-state mirrors have been removed. Initial rendering
and the supplementary browser Tasks caller remain unchanged.

The complete [Todo Browser caller](../../../examples/todo-browser/src/lib.rs) constructs the graph, reduces typed Todo commands, commits keyed DOM changes and owns its disposal lifetime. Follow [Todo's browser setup](../../../examples/todo-server/README.md) or, from the repository root:

```bash
cargo xtask build browser
cargo run --locked -p yetlet-todo-server
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000/app`; the local toggle uses the graph and the server Create action uses a separate HTTP executor. Browser build prerequisites are in the sample guide. A native caller can use the graph without any browser dependency.

## Ownership and failures

`State` must be `Clone + 'static`; messages, error values and captured callbacks also require the documented static lifetimes. The graph uses `Rc`/`RefCell` and is local to one thread. One non-cloneable strong owner controls its lifetime; `GraphHandle` and `Subscription` are weak. Dropping the owner or calling `dispose()` releases owned captures; dispatch and snapshot afterwards return `ReactiveError::Disposed`. Snapshot returns `ReactiveError::Faulted` for a live faulted graph, with disposal taking precedence. Dropping or unsubscribing a subscription removes its observer.

Messages are FIFO, with one successful commit/notification per pass. Dispatch during commit/observation queues a later pass. The default limit is 64 passes; `with_pass_limit` requires a positive limit and panics on zero. Reducer errors keep the prior state and remain recoverable. Commit errors and pass exhaustion fault the graph; dispose and rebuild it before reuse. External effects performed by callbacks are not transactionally undone.

This is not dependency-tracked signals, automatic effects, async scheduling, generic forms or resumability. Retained [M7g evidence](../../../docs/M7G-VERIFICATION.md) and [the lifecycle decision](../../../docs/adr/0007-bounded-keyed-dom-and-local-graph.md) describe the bounded selection.

# Experimental native secret providers

`yetlet::secrets` is an unpublished, explicit native module of the shared SDK. Its only runtime dependency is `secrecy`. It does not register with
Yetlet Core, App, configuration, the CLI, or browser code. Browser WASM is rejected.

`SecretProvider: Send + Sync` exposes object-safe asynchronous
`get(name) -> Result<Option<SecretString>, SecretError>` through a boxed Send
future. Applications inject `Arc<dyn SecretProvider>` into their own ordinary
service constructors or Axum/Yetlet state. Replace that value to select a custom
implementation; no provider registry or DI container is required.

`Ok(None)` means a genuinely missing name. `Unavailable` and `AccessDenied` are
distinct failures with fixed public messages and no backend error sources.
Names are exact and case-sensitive. Empty and whitespace-only strings remain
present values; required-value validation belongs to the consumer.

```rust
use std::{collections::BTreeMap, sync::Arc};
use yetlet::secrets::{SecretProvider, SettingsSecrets};

// `settings` was already loaded by the application's existing Loader.
let settings_provider = Arc::new(SettingsSecrets::new(
    BTreeMap::from([("delivery-token".into(), settings.service.token)]),
));
let provider: Arc<dyn SecretProvider> = settings_provider.clone();
// Pass `provider` into an ordinary service constructor or app-owned state.

// After explicitly reloading settings with the same application Loader:
settings_provider.replace(BTreeMap::from([
    ("delivery-token".into(), reloaded.service.token),
]))?;
```

`SettingsSecrets` owns a snapshot of only the selected fields. Its explicit
`replace(values)` replaces the whole selected map through `&self`, so existing
shared handles observe new values on subsequent lookups. Include every name to
retain; omitted names become missing. Each lookup sees a complete old or new
snapshot, but separate lookups are not an atomic transaction. The adapter uses a
short synchronous lock, holds no lock across await or I/O, and returns the fixed
`Unavailable` error if that lock is poisoned.
There is no revision check: replacing identical values is allowed, and any
supplied map can replace the previous one. If an application offers reload,
serialize the full load, app validation, selection and replacement through one
app-owned entry, acquiring its gate before any input read. Loading/validation
failure skips replacement and retains the healthy snapshot. Every writer must
use that entry; the provider's own lock only serializes publication. This does
not prevent external source rollback or coordinate other processes. Restart
loads current inputs with no persisted version history.
It reads no files or environment variables, does not reflect over all settings,
and does not change existing settings or development-secret precedence. Its Debug
output omits both keys and values. Each successful lookup returns an owned
protected clone; exposing it requires an explicit `ExposeSecret` call. Do not put
secret values in logs, errors, HTML, JSON, or serialized hydration state. Protected
strings do not prevent an application from leaking an explicitly exposed value,
and the existing loader still handles intermediate configuration text normally.

Lookup timing is application policy. `get` never generates, rotates or reloads a
credential. To adopt a local file/environment change, the application explicitly
reruns its existing Loader, selects secret fields and calls `replace`. Generic
credential rotation also requires updating the external source and its consumers;
replacement is only the local adoption step. An already returned `SecretString`
or a client that copied its credential keeps the old value. Applications must
explicitly reconfigure or rebuild those clients. This slice adds no cloud SDK,
remote provider, secret writer, cache, watcher, retry, or automatic rotation.

The listener-free [state example](../examples/config/secrets_state.rs) loads typed app-owned
`service.token`, explicitly maps it to `delivery-token`, constructs an ordinary
service with the provider, and installs that service in app-owned Axum/Yetlet
state. The public page uses only a selected public message. It makes no external
request and implements no authentication. The Development fixture contains only
a synthetic placeholder. The default Production fixture inherits an empty token
and the example reports HTTP 503; a runtime override supplies a configured value:

```sh
YTSECRETS_SERVICE__TOKEN="${YTSECRETS_SERVICE__TOKEN:?Set a local test value first}" cargo run --offline --locked \
  -p yetlet --features config --example config-secrets-state --features secret-provider,server-axum
```

For an explicit local development secret file, application startup can retain the
existing `Loader::development_secrets(path, SecretFormat::Toml)` or Dotenv API
before `.load()`. Select Development with `YTSECRETS_ENVIRONMENT=Development`.
Staging and Production ignore that development file selection. Base settings,
the selected profile, the explicit Development secret file, then environment
overrides retain their existing order. No new secret namespace or parser exists.

The example's tests exercise those layers with synthetic values, both ignored
development-file profiles, explicit v1-to-v2 file reload into the same service's
provider, custom provider substitution, and escaped SSR with CSP and no secret
output. They also demonstrate a single application-owned reload gate around
loading, validation and publication, concurrent reload ordering, and preservation
of the old snapshot on failed reload followed by recovery. The executable still
loads once at startup; no reload loop or provider administration is installed.
The provider tests cover whole-map replacement through shared handles,
retained owned values, empty/missing distinctions, Send execution, fixed poison
errors, protected ownership, and redacted Debug/errors.

The State example and its four fixtures now belong to `yetlet::config`, behind
its existing `secret-provider` feature. Run that target with `cargo test --offline
--locked -p yetlet --features config --example config-secrets-state
--features secret-provider,server-axum`. The provider-only commands below do not run the
moved composition target. This removes the reverse Config development dependency
for first publication without changing provider APIs or runtime dependencies.

```sh
cargo test --offline --locked -p yetlet --features secrets --all-targets
cargo test --offline --locked -p yetlet --features secrets --doc
cargo clippy --offline --locked -p yetlet --features secrets --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

The original read-contract evidence was local native only. The separately
selected [rotation, Windows and Azure record](../../../docs/SECRET-ROTATION-VERIFICATION.md)
covers explicit replacement and the read-only Azure CLI experiment in
`examples/azure_cli.rs`. It does not establish production cloud-provider or
secret-management guarantees.

See the [local inputs and administration contract](../../../docs/SECRET-PROVIDERS.md)
for the existing settings sources and the separation between application reads,
operator/automation rotation, signing and TLS certificate renewal.

# yetlet::server_axum

Build native HTML pages and JSON endpoints with a small facade over Axum/Tower.
The server adapter does not install browser, Session or configuration capabilities.

**Experimental, unpublished.** Use this source checkout and the documented target scope.


## Prerequisites

Use this checkout with Rust/Cargo 1.99.0 and prepared locked dependencies, or allow
Cargo to fetch them. Run the example below from the repository root. No Node.js,
WASM target or optional provider is required for this path.

## Minimal integration

### Start a native page and JSON API

From the repository root, run the existing complete example:

```bash
cargo run --locked -p yetlet --features server-axum --example server-axum-minimal
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` and `/api/status`. The code below is copied verbatim from [minimal.rs](../examples/server_axum/minimal.rs):

```rust
use yetlet::view::View;
use yetlet::server_axum::{App, response::Json};

async fn home() -> View {
    View::text("Hello from Yetlet")
}
async fn status() -> Json<&'static str> {
    Json("ready")
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let app: axum::Router = App::new()
        .page("/", "Yetlet", home)
        .group("/api", |api| api.get("/status", status))
        .into_router();
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:3000").await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

## Expected result

The example serves HTML at `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` and JSON at `/api/status`.
`Page` produces escaped complete documents with the default strict CSP. Ctrl+C
stops the foreground listener; a Router setup alone does not bind a listener.

## Configuration and errors

### Native interoperability

`App<S>` is a thin facade; `into_router()` returns a native Axum Router. `.page(path, title, handler)` accepts a no-argument async View handler. Parameterized/fallible handlers use `.get`, native `Path`, `Query`, `State` or `Json`, and return `Page` or `Result<Page, E>`. Native JSON, redirects, statuses and headers retain Axum semantics. `configure`/`try_configure` execute ordinary typed setup functions during construction, without Controllers, DI, plugin discovery or a second model binder.

`RequestContext<S>` owns request parts/body and typed request extensions separately from application state. Native middleware remains usable directly; `with_global` wraps a fully assembled Router before routing. Follow [HTTP pipeline ordering/body semantics](../../../docs/HTTP-PIPELINE.md) when composing layers. SQL/storage remain application-owned choices.

### Documents and errors

`Page::new`, `render_document` and `render_page` use the legacy `zh-Hant` root language. For another language, validate `LanguageTag` and select `DocumentMetadata` with `Page::with_metadata` or the metadata-aware render functions. The contract is title/language plus fixed charset/viewport; no arbitrary head DSL is installed. Language validation is conservative ASCII shape validation, not a complete BCP 47 registry.

Views are escaped through `yetlet::html`. Rendering errors become a generic HTTP 500 through `Page`/`HtmlPageError`; HTML responses carry the strict default CSP. Full SSR buffers the document and needs no JS/WASM. Browser assets/loaders are explicitly application-owned build outputs. [Streaming](../../../docs/YT-021-STREAMING-SSR-RESEARCH.md) and [deadline](../../../docs/YT-029-HTTP-DEADLINE-RESEARCH.md) research remain app-owned opt-ins, without a core streaming/suspense/deadline API.

## API reference

Use the [source/rustdoc entry](../src/server_axum/mod.rs) and [current API reference](../../../docs/API-REFERENCE.md).
Native upstream routing and extraction contracts remain Axum/Tower-owned.

### License and compatibility

Dual-licensed under [MIT](../../../LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](../../../LICENSE-APACHE). The privately prepared `0.1.x` policy preserves documented behavior and Rust 1.99 in patches; public activation remains blocked. See [compatibility](../../../docs/COMPATIBILITY.md), [API classifications](../../../docs/API-CONTRACTS.md) and [developer guides](../../../docs/README.md). Links to companion packages and records assume this checkout; they do not imply public hosting or distribution.

`yetlet::server_axum` adapts Yetlet Views to ordinary Axum/Tower HTTP applications. Dependencies are Axum, Tower, serde, `yetlet::view` and `yetlet::html`; browser runtime, Session and request correlation are not installed.

# Experimental Valkey / Redis-protocol Session provider — YT-066b2

**Status: focused integration tests and independent implementation review passed at bounded YT-066b2 scope. Do not treat this crate as production-qualified.** See [provider implementation verification](../../../docs/YT-066B2-VERIFICATION.md) and the later [three-application qualification](../../../docs/YT-066B3-VERIFICATION.md). It is unpublished and has its own workspace/lockfile, outside the default framework build and dependency graphs. The existing synchronous Memory provider is unchanged.

This is a separate, explicitly selected async Session implementation, not an authentication system. It uses the reviewed single-primary Lua semantics and [selected pure-SSR Cookie contract](../../../docs/YT-066B-COOKIE-ORDERING.md). No JavaScript, plugin registry, DI container, implicit Memory fallback or synchronous Redis facade is added.

This package is included in the selected sixteen-package experimental 0.9.0-alpha.5
candidate. It remains unpublished; candidate selection and publication-prepared
metadata do not establish registry availability or expand the support scope.

The later [YT-094 Valkey reference](../../../docs/YT-094-VALKEY-SESSIONS.md) selects
Valkey 9.1.2 for actual two-app shared-session verification. It reuses this
implementation and existing protocol/key schema. Its later TTL correction
accepts up to 30 days, matching the Memory provider's upper bound; the other
experimental bounds remain unchanged. The historical crate/API names remain compatible; the
reference's feature and backend setting use `valkey`. This evidence does not
upgrade the provider to a production or HA guarantee.

## API and application responsibilities

- Construct `RedisSessionConfig::new(namespace, cookie_scope, ttl, max_in_flight, payload_limit)` and explicitly connect `RedisSessionManager::<T>::connect(endpoint, config).await`. The endpoint is never included in provider errors/Debug. Default mode accepts `redis://`. The optional `session-redis-tls` feature additionally admits checked `rediss://` using native Rustls/Ring and native trust roots; insecure URL fragments reject. Deployment/ACL/recovery qualification remains separately scoped.
- `manager.scoped(app)` applies native Axum middleware only to existing routes. `Extension<RedisSession<T>>` or the typed request extension exposes the handle. Routes outside the scope are independent.
- `open` only parses the configured cookie. `read().await` always loads authoritative Redis state; missing/invalid state never silently creates a Session. An application must explicitly call `create(value).await` after its own policy checks. An active identity requires `replace_and_rotate` instead of another create.
- `try_update(|state| Result<R, E>).await` invokes the closure once, commits by CAS and returns its original `R` only after acknowledged success. Application rejection writes nothing. Conflict is explicit; callbacks are never automatically replayed. A synchronous callback must not block the async executor; external side effects are not rolled back.
- `rotate`, `replace_and_rotate` and `destroy` are async, atomic identity operations. `csrf_token` and constant-time `verify_csrf` authoritatively load the record; applications must enforce CSRF and authorization for their own unsafe actions. Session creation alone does not authenticate anyone.
- `OutcomeUnknown` carries a redacted `RedisOperationId`. `resolve_operation` returns historical status only; it neither retries the write, reconstructs arbitrary `R`, nor grants access to a retired identity. Cancellation may lose a ticket before the caller receives it.
- Call `shutdown().await` during application shutdown. It stops admission across clones and drains/reaps owned work. Dropping a request future is not proof that a write was cancelled.

`T` explicitly requires serde serialization/deserialization plus Clone/Send/Sync; the existing Memory provider gains no serialization bound. JSON is an opaque state field under schema 2, not a stable wire format. Unsupported/corrupt data fails closed; there is no migration/reset fallback. The internal issuance metadata is retained from the prototype but does not participate in cookie names or identity selection.

## Cookie behavior

The default cookie has one `__Host-` name, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/ and no Domain. Only the explicit local HTTP override uses a distinct insecure name. Malformed/duplicate configured-name cookies fail closed and legacy issuance names are ignored.

Only successful create/rotate/replace can leave a pending Set. A successful subsequent update in the same request preserves that creation/rotation directive; an ordinary loaded-session read/update does not mint or refresh a cookie. Error responses and destroy emit no Set/Clear. Finalization resolves the operation and reloads/decodes its current identity before adding the cookie. Middleware finalizer failure returns a redacted 503; malformed Cookie headers return 400. Application handlers choose their own Session-error HTTP mapping.

A late prepared Set may overwrite a newer cookie and require login again. The authoritative store must reject retired/revoked/expired credentials. No old-ID forwarding, alternate-cookie selection or global latest-login/account policy is provided. Logout revokes server state without a clearing response; a dead cookie may remain until overwrite/expiry. The prior Cookie prototype passed its independent review, but that PASS does not certify this new integration.

## Deliberate bounds and unqualified scope

Configuration accepts a 1–64 character isolated namespace, a 1–20 character cookie scope, 1 ms–30 days absolute Session lifetime, 1–4 in-flight calls plus the same number of waiters, and 1–4096 bytes encoded payload. Sub-millisecond lifetime precision is truncated. The caller chooses the lifetime; the Admin reference defaults to 30 minutes through settings. Reads and CAS updates do not renew expiry, while rotation starts a new configured lifetime. Reuse the same namespace/config for workers sharing one application; choose a new namespace when intentionally invalidating all prior state.

The fixed experimental bounds are: 400 ms shared caller deadline across request-lock/queue/Redis phases, 80 ms operation queue wait, 200 ms connect timeout, one reconnect retry with 10–20 ms backoff, immutable one-second server dispatch window, five-second operation-result retention, 64 result records per namespace, 400 ms tombstones and two-second shutdown drain. A synchronous callback cannot be interrupted; if it exhausts the caller deadline, the next phase refuses dispatch. Caller timeout does not cancel a dispatched Redis write; owned work retains its permits until a reply/disconnect or shutdown.

Lua script isolation is not rollback on runtime/OOM failure. Later [YT-066b3 qualification](../../../docs/YT-066B3-VERIFICATION.md) passed actual three-application execution, owned cleanup and independent review at single-host/single-primary/no-persistence scope. YT-066 is Done at that recorded scope; this isolated provider remains outside the historical nine-package immutable candidate. The later TLS/ACL and cross-host/persistent-restart evidence below has its own bounded inputs; neither record qualifies arbitrary restore, HA/Cluster or application SLO/RPO/RTO. YT-020 remains Blocked and no registry upload is authorized. Never restore an older namespace and assume revoked credentials remain invalid.

## Local checks

Compile and lint without Redis:

```sh
CARGO_TARGET_DIR="$PWD/target/yt066b2-build" cargo +1.99.0 test -p yetlet --features session-redis --locked --no-run
CARGO_TARGET_DIR="$PWD/target/yt066b2-build" cargo clippy -p yetlet --features session-redis --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

Remote-service tests are ignored unless explicitly selected; the configuration test needs no service. Use only a disposable [Redis fixture](../../../qualification/yt066b/compose.yaml) or the [Valkey fixture](../../../qualification/yt094-valkey/README.md), random loopback listener and exact-project cleanup. They deliberately pause writes and corrupt synthetic records. Do not run against a shared store. The CAS test uses `block_in_place` for its synchronous callback barrier. Historical provider tests passed after that test-only correction; the separate cancellation/drain test retains its earlier PASS. The verification record preserves both prior stalled attempts and the explicitly authorized correction. The added TTL integration checks a 30-minute store TTL/cookie, non-sliding reads/updates and cross-manager rotation/logout.


## Separate admission-burst research

[YT-172](../../../docs/YT-172-SESSION-ADMISSION-BURSTS.md) adds one ignored,
`cfg(test)`-only provider-read study. Normal builds contain no probe, timer,
capture or public API. It retains the existing four active/eight total slots
and all deadlines/security semantics; it is not an HTTP capacity qualification.
The explicit native test filter is
`store::admission_probe::session_admission_burst_research`, with
`--lib --release --offline --locked` and `-- --ignored --exact --nocapture
--test-threads=1`. Set `YT172_SESSION_URL` only to a dedicated disposable
loopback Valkey and `YT172_OUTPUT` to an excluded private JSON path. Follow the
contract's fixed cases, no-replay and exact-owned cleanup rules. Contract and
corrected mapping pass; the one new probe validates 552 reads and retains 96
barrier-wave busy rejections, with eight successful serial recovery reads. Actual
resource absence is verified; initial startup/mapping and already-unloaded-unit
cleanup failures remain in the report. Final independent Reviewer PASS has zero
issues/required followups; YT-172 is Done at bounded provider-research scope.


## Separate full-HTTP timeline research

[YT-173](../../../docs/YT-173-HTTP-SESSION-TIMELINE.md) uses the explicit private
compiler cfg `yetlet_session_admission_probe` to link fixture HTTP scopes and
provider/worker timing on one process-local clock. The hidden linkage module
is an unsupported research-build interface; ordinary builds have no export,
probe state, timer or capture. No Cargo feature/dependency, gate size, deadline,
worker ownership or security semantics changes. Never use its synthetic request
tag for authentication or policy. Follow the fixed study/cleanup contract and
retain timing-boundary/observer limits. Contract and focused checks pass;
corrected mapping and the one new HTTP study pass: twelve busy requests have
eight proven slot owners (four active/four pending), with complete correlated
records and actual cleanup. Original failures/uncertainty remain; final independent
Reviewer PASS has zero issues/required followups, Done at bounded research scope.


## Optional native TLS — YT-184 reference

Select `features = ["session-redis-tls"]` explicitly and supply `rediss://` through a trusted
private input. The existing connect API, Session/Lua/admission semantics and
errors stay unchanged. No TLS backend is installed for the default graph.
The feature selects the mature native Rustls/Ring backend, standard certificate/
hostname verification and TLS1.2/1.3, with native trust roots; it rejects insecure
URL fragments rather than accepting a verification bypass. Applications own
trust-root selection, server authentication/ACL, secret input and lifecycle. The
application identity needs direct `TIME` permission: `Store::prepare` reads the
server clock before a mutation, separately from Lua execution. A namespace-
scoped deployment ACL using connection/scripting/read/write categories must
explicitly add `+time`; those categories alone do not grant it. The YT-184
fixture initially omitted this permission. The opt-in regression
`yt184_named_acl_time_grant_unblocks_session_lifecycle` now reproduces the refusal
with a password-authenticated app/default user disabled, then verifies the
unchanged provider lifecycle after only `+time`. That local router/TCP test is
separate from pending Azure Auth/restart qualification.
Endpoints/passwords must not be printed or serialized. No custom crypto, parser,
public factory or automatic upgrade of a plaintext endpoint is added.

The [YT-184 isolated cross-host contract](../../../docs/YT-184-AZURE-AUTH-SESSION-RESTART.md)
selects task-CA roots only in fresh owned guests, private authenticated Valkey
and SQL, Secure cookies and explicit new-epoch re-login after authority restart.
Its first cloud bootstrap fails at a Path expression; authorized generation2
reaches both apps READY and rejects wrong SQL/Valkey TLS names, then fails the
SQL observer before the Auth/restart journey. Both failed generations are fully
deleted; the observer is corrected locally. These are historical failed attempts; the current composed reference is accepted
at bounded YT-184 scope after final Reviewer PASS, with YT-184 Done. Earlier single-host/
no-persistence qualification remains historical; this optional transport does
not establish general production, HA, arbitrary restore or platform coverage.


Native connection recovery may first surface a dropped or failed-reconnect error
and initiate background reconnection. A fixed sleep or server-process READY
alone is not per-client availability. YT-184's local persistent restart case
records this behavior using read-only observations; it adds no provider automatic
mutation replay or stronger recovery/SLO guarantee. Cross-host Auth/policy/logout
passes in generation4; generation5 completes authority recovery/VM restart,
accepted after final independent Reviewer PASS at bounded reference scope.


YT-184 is Done at bounded reference scope after final independent Reviewer PASS:
generation4 Auth and generation5 remaining authority recovery/persistent VM
restart with native exit0. Full SQL/restrictive policy, unexpired old-epoch
refusal and fresh-login/durable-output/logout checks pass; transient503s and
all earlier failures remain retained. All five groups/credentials are deleted.
This isolated Linux reference does not qualify HA, arbitrary restore or other
platforms; see the contract for exact composition and remaining acceptance.

# yetlet::session

Add bounded, process-local Memory Session state, cookie lifecycle and explicit
CSRF checks to a native application. Session can be anonymous and is not authentication.

**Experimental, unpublished.** Use this source checkout and the documented target scope.


## Prerequisites

Use this checkout with Rust/Cargo 1.99.0. The runnable cart selects native Session
explicitly and requires no JS/WASM or remote store. Run from the repository root;
allow locked dependency downloads unless the Cargo cache is already prepared.

## Minimal integration

### Use the native Session cart

From the repository root:

```bash
cargo run --locked -p yetlet-cart-server
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:3002/cart`; forms work without JS/WASM. The [complete cart implementation](../../../examples/cart-server/src/lib.rs) and [sample guide](../../../examples/cart-server/README.md) demonstrate configuration, scoped registration, reads, fallible updates, CSRF validation, rotation and destruction. The demo explicitly permits insecure cookies only on loopback HTTP.

For your own app, validate `SessionConfig::new(cookie_name, ttl, max_sessions)`, construct `SessionManager::<T>::new(config)`, then apply `manager.scoped(app)` after registering the intended routes. Handlers extract `Extension<Session<T>>` or the typed request extension. `T` requires `Default + Clone + Send + 'static`, with no serde bound. Cloned managers share their store; independent managers do not. Session handles share request-local identity/cookie directives and must stay within the owning request's application lifetime.

## Expected result

At `http://127.0.0.1:3002/cart`, native forms update the selected Session without
browser code. The demo deliberately selects loopback-only insecure HTTP cookies.
Independent managers/processes do not share this Memory store; restart loses it.

## Configuration and errors

### Cookies, mutations and failures

Cookie defaults are Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Path=/, with no Domain. `insecure_for_local_http()` is an explicit demo override; production apps retain Secure and select their TLS/proxy policy. Missing/unknown/expired identities create a new default Session within capacity rather than adopting a caller-supplied ID. Expiry is absolute rather than sliding.

`read()` clones state. `try_update` mutates a clone and commits only on `Ok`; it distinguishes Session failures from application rejection. Callbacks run synchronously under store ownership: keep them short and non-blocking, and do not assume external effects roll back. `rotate` and `replace_and_rotate` retire the identity and rotate CSRF; `destroy` removes server state and expires the cookie. `csrf_token` and constant-time `verify_csrf` support explicit application enforcement; they do not install authorization.

Invalid configuration returns `SessionConfigError`; TTL is 1 second–30 days and capacity is 1–1,000,000. Session operations can fail with `Unavailable`, `Expired` or `Destroyed`. Middleware rejects malformed cookies with 400 and capacity/entropy/store failures with 503; handlers choose how to map their own operation/application failures.

### Deployment boundary

Session is not authentication or durable storage. Restart loses Memory state; multiple independent processes do not share it. Logout/cookie response reordering requires application-aware handling, and CSRF tokens must be checked on unsafe actions. Avoid serializing identities, tokens or server capabilities into browser state.

The [separate experimental Redis-protocol provider](session-redis.md)
has publication-prepared metadata and is included in the selected sixteen-package
candidate, but remains unpublished. Its async, single-primary semantics and
separately recorded Valkey evidence do not broaden Memory guarantees or imply
generic HA/failover/restore support. See [provider operations](../../../docs/PROVIDER-OPERATIONS.md)
and the provider guide for its current limits; [M8c evidence](../../../docs/M8C-VERIFICATION.md)
retains the earlier Memory scope.

## API reference

Use [Session source/rustdoc](../src/session/mod.rs), the complete cart linked above and
the [current API reference](../../../docs/API-REFERENCE.md).

### License and compatibility

Dual-licensed under [MIT](../../../LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](../../../LICENSE-APACHE). The privately prepared `0.1.x` policy preserves documented behavior and Rust 1.99 in patches; public activation remains blocked. See [compatibility](../../../docs/COMPATIBILITY.md), [API classifications](../../../docs/API-CONTRACTS.md) and [developer guides](../../../docs/README.md). Links to companion packages and records assume this checkout; they do not imply public hosting or distribution.

<summary>Historical delivery context and evidence</summary>

**Experimental `0.9.0-alpha.5`, unpublished.** Requires Rust 1.99 or newer. This is one of Yetlet's sixteen library candidates; use the local checkout rather than assuming a registry release. APIs are pre-public, and bounded prototype verification is not production qualification.

`yetlet::session` is an opt-in, synchronous process-local Memory Session provider. It owns random opaque identities, bounded in-memory values, absolute expiry, cookie lifecycle and session-bound CSRF tokens. It depends on Axum, cookie, getrandom, subtle and `yetlet::server_axum`; no browser runtime or Redis dependency is added.

# yetlet::signing

Experimental, unpublished `0.9.0-alpha.5` release preparation. Requires Rust 1.99+ and
a native OpenSSL development/runtime configuration compatible with the pinned
Rust bindings. Select this package explicitly; Core/HTML/browser consumers do
not acquire it automatically. Publication eligibility does not activate release
signing, certificates, public logs or a registry upload.

## Prerequisites

Use this checkout until a public release is separately approved. The selected
reference is GNU/Linux; Windows, macOS and browser Wasm are not qualified by
this package preparation. YT-093's native evidence uses an isolated static
OpenSSL 3.5.9 build with `openssl 0.10.81` / `openssl-sys 0.9.117`; that is a
recorded recipe, not a promise that every installed OpenSSL is compatible.

## Minimal integration

```rust
use yetlet::signing::Sha256Digest;

let digest = Sha256Digest::of(b"explicit application bytes");
assert_eq!(digest.0.len(), 32);
```

The example hashes exact bytes. It does not select a signing identity, generate

trust; pin and policy decisions remain explicit. Certificate leaf checks are
not general PKI chain/revocation validation or trusted signing-time evidence.
Local state exposes no mandatory network, filesystem service or automatic key
rotation. Protect private material and passwords in the consuming application.

Typed errors distinguish invalid material/signature, unknown key, unsupported
algorithm, rejected policy and unavailable backend, without exposing raw native
diagnostics. Provider adapters and actual production custody are separate choices.
